synopsis: The booklet recommends starting with a narrow reverse-only, low-speed wheel-loader operating domain: Volvo CE’s January 2023 system operates at 3–15 km/h and brakes for 2–3 seconds, while Caterpillar’s medium-wheel-loader system also targets reverse operation [f11397, f1238, f356]. Reversing risk is population-specific: 67% of 22 US surface-mine blind-area fatalities from 2000 to mid-2006 involved the rear blind area of reversing equipment, but the booklet identifies forward motion or starting from rest as the deadliest haul-truck pattern [f2986, f2993, f11409]. US construction and metal/non-metal mining rules require reverse alarms, observers or specified alternatives when rear visibility is obstructed; ISO 21815-3:2023 covers both forward and reverse warning and avoidance through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition, not automatic steering [f2228, f2237, f2163]. The 2006 NIOSH study recorded 580 alarms over 618 reversals during seven days of testing: 102 were false alarms (18%), 243 nuisance alarms (42%), and only 235 actionable alarms (41%), highlighting alarm-quality concerns [f5436, f5174, f5175]. Virtual validation has a critical close-range gap because workers 0.5–5 m behind machines occupy the range where digital radar simulators are weakest, although AGX Dynamics for Unity added a lidar-based reverse auto-brake example on 4 April 2025 [f5328, f8573]. Planning should account for reversal requests, transmission delays and opposite-direction collision risks, while treating coverage of reversing trailers under draft ISO 21815 Part 5 as provisional, with publication planned for November 2026 [f6338, f6039, f6747].
